title: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre: Masterpiece
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the 1974 horror film The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, often called a masterpiece. They cover its inspirations (Ed Gein, a med student's cadaver-mask story, a Montgomery Ward chainsaw), script writing by Kim Henkel and Toby Hooper, the title suggested by Warren Skaggs-style film commissioner Warren Scarin, the low budget and cast of unknowns, a detailed plot walkthrough (the van, Last Chance Gas, the Hardesty homestead, Leatherface, the dinner scene, the ending on the highway), the brutal shoot in Texas heat, the Brianston distribution deal tied to Colombo crime family money, the X-to-R rating fight, the film's critical reception and legacy, sequels and remakes, and a listener email about a black night at a roller rink.

segments.title: Opening and spoiler warning
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Halloween-week episode, warn about spoilers and gruesome content, and say the film is worth watching regardless of horror taste.

segments.title: Why the film is considered a masterpiece
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh describe how disturbing the film feels to them, with Josh noting it works as a dark comedy and Chuck finding it terrifying; they note the film was made by young students and is considered a masterpiece.

segments.title: Inspirations: Ed Gein, a cadaver mask, and a chainsaw
segments.summary: Toby Hooper drew on serial killer Ed Gein, a med student friend's claim of wearing a cadaver face mask, and a crowded Montgomery Ward store where he saw chainsaws, with Hansel and Gretel as a loose influence. The hosts note their earlier Ed Gein episode.
topics: Psycho and Silence of the Lambs influence

segments.title: Writing the script and the title
segments.summary: Toby Hooper and Kim Henkel wrote the script together quickly, mapping the story on the floor. Working titles included Head Cheese. Warren Scarin, Texas's first film commissioner, came up with the final title. The hosts discuss the 2017 Leatherface prequel and a later reboot being developed by A24.

segments.title: Budget and early financing
segments.summary: The budget was pitched at sixty thousand dollars, with forty and twenty thousand alternatives. Bill Parsley, a former Texas state legislator, was the first investor. The final cost reached about three hundred thousand dollars, mostly from Parsley and other investors.

segments.title: Casting unknown actors and cutting costs
segments.summary: The filmmakers hired inexperienced actors, some drama students from UT Austin, and got them to defer pay. Jim Siedow was the only experienced actor, with radio soap experience. John Larroquette had an uncredited voice role, paid in pot, and his first film work.

segments.title: Marilyn Burns and Susan Sarandon's body double
segments.summary: Marilyn Burns had prior credits including Brewster McCloud and was cast as lead in Love and Molly before being replaced by Susan Sarandon, for whom she later became a body double.

segments.title: Opening narration and setup
segments.summary: The docudrama-style opening narration by John Larroquette is read aloud. The story is set on October 18, 1973, and the friends go to a cemetery where grave robbing has occurred, then look for their grandfather's grave.

segments.title: Plot: last chance gas, the hitchhiker, Kirk's death
segments.summary: The friends stop at a run-down gas station and barbecue pit called Last Chance Gas, which is out of gas. They pick up the hitchhiker Nubbins Sawyer, who cuts himself and slashes Franklin, and they push him out. At the Hardesty homestead, Kirk goes to a nearby house looking for gas and is killed by Leatherface with a hammer.

segments.title: Plot: Pam, Jerry, and Franklin's death
segments.summary: Pam goes looking for Kirk and is hung on a meat hook; Jerry searches for them and is killed with one hammer swing. Pam is in a freezer. Franklin and Sally go into the woods, where Leatherface kills Franklin in his wheelchair.

segments.title: Plot: Sally's escape and the dinner scene
segments.summary: Sally runs to the Sawyer house and escapes through a window, then is captured by Drayton at the gas station and beaten with a broom. At the dinner scene, Leatherface cuts her finger so Grandpa can drink her blood, and Grandpa's failed hammer blows nearly kill her.

segments.title: Plot: the highway ending
segments.summary: Sally escapes through a window and runs down the driveway with Nubbins chasing her. A tractor-trailer named Black Maria runs over Nubbins, and the driver, played by Ed Gwenn, throws a pipe wrench that wounds Leatherface. A pickup driven by Perry Lorenz takes Sally, and the film cuts to black.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Shooting locations and brutal conditions
segments.summary: The film was shot in about 31 days in mid-July to mid-August 1973 in suburbs around Austin, Round Rock and Bastrop, at about six locations. Shooting was without permits for the road scenes, in heat around 100 degrees, and the Sawyer house was hotter inside.

segments.title: Meat themes and set conditions
segments.summary: Production designer Bob Burns used Ed Gein crime scene photos for set decoration. The house smelled from real meat, and cast members threw up between takes. Long shooting days, one chainsaw, and pressure from financier Bill Parsley marked the shoot.

segments.title: Tension on set and actor treatment
segments.summary: Toby Hooper stoked tension among the cast. Gunnar Hansen was isolated and each victim actor first met him on screen. Paul Partain stayed in character and was disliked. Marilyn Burns did most of her own stunts, and Jim Siedow was pressured into hitting her with the broom.

segments.title: Blood on set and filmmaking techniques
segments.summary: Marilyn Burns really was cut on the finger for the dinner scene because the blood squib failed. Daniel Pearl, cinematographer age 23, was hired after a Texas DPS drug-bust PSA. The crew built their own dollies and crane. Editors Larry Carroll and Sally Richardson shaped the pacing.

segments.title: Financing, Brianston distribution, and money
segments.summary: Investors were added as the budget grew, and Hooper and Henkel gave up shares, leaving them with 15% combined. Film commissioner Warren Scarin shopped the film. Brianston Distributing, linked to the Colombo crime family, released it. Cast and crew got about $8,100 to split, and investors sued before Brianston went bankrupt. New Line picked it up in 1983.

segments.title: MPAA rating fight and marketing
segments.summary: Hooper wanted a PG rating but the MPAA's board gave the meat hook scene an X. He lobbied it down to an R. Brianston used publicity and controversy as marketing. The film was placed in the Museum of Modern Art collection.

segments.title: Reception, gross, and legacy
segments.summary: Critics initially panned the film, though Roger Ebert and Rex Reed were discussed. The film grossed about $26 million in its year, and about $150 million in current money, and was once called the most successful independent film. Quentin Tarantino and Stanley Kubrick praised it. The final girl trope and slasher origins were discussed alongside Black Christmas.

segments.title: Sequels, remakes, and comparisons
segments.summary: Hosts discuss that many sequels and remakes exist, that none match the original, and mention Rob Zombie's House of 1000 Corpses, Wolf Creek, and the Maxine trilogy (X, Pearl). John Landis compared the 2003 remake to a shampoo commercial.

segments.title: Chuck watching the film plan
segments.summary: Josh says he will watch Chuck watch the film together, which triggers the listener mail segment.

segments.title: Listener mail from Tequarius
segments.summary: Listener Tequarius McMurray writes about a black night at a skating rink when he was thirteen and sends a photo. Josh thanks him and invites more listener mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes with the show's iHeartRadio production credit and a pointer to other podcasts.
